pharm: Tricyclic-structured central muscle relaxant that reduces tonic somatic motor activity via brainstem action; relieves acute muscle spasm.
quick: 5 mg three times daily (may increase to 10 mg TID)
Limited data; use only if clearly needed
Reduce dose/frequency; avoid in moderate-severe impairment
summary: Cyclobenzaprine is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant for short-term relief of muscle spasm in acute, painful musculoskeletal conditions, used as an adjunct to rest and physical therapy. It is structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants and shares their sedative and anticholinergic effects. Use is limited to 2-3 weeks. It is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors, in hyperthyroidism, and in several cardiac conditions.
indications: Adjunct to rest and physical therapy for relief of muscle spasm associated with acute, painful musculoskeletal conditions

dosage.n: May increase to 10 mg three times a day based on response
Start low; avoid in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment

admin: Take by mouth with or without food
Start with lower/less frequent dosing in elderly and hepatic impairment
Combine with rest and physical therapy
Avoid abrupt high doses due to sedation
moa: Acts primarily at the brainstem (rather than spinal cord or muscle directly) to reduce tonic somatic motor activity, relieving skeletal muscle spasm of local origin without impairing muscle function. Structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants with associated anticholinergic and sedative effects.

absolute: Concomitant MAO inhibitor use or within 14 days of discontinuation
Acute recovery phase of myocardial infarction
Arrhythmias, heart block, conduction disturbances, or congestive heart failure
relative: History of urinary retention, angle-closure glaucoma, increased intraocular pressure

preg: Limited data; use only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: Closely related to tricyclic antidepressants which are excreted in milk; use with caution during breastfeeding.
hepatic: Plasma levels are increased; use lower starting dose and less frequent dosing in mild impairment and avoid in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment.

major: MAO inhibitors - risk of hyperpyretic crisis, seizures, death (contraindicated)
Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, triptans, linezolid) - serotonin syndrome risk
moderate: CNS depressants and alcohol - additive sedation
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; enhances CNS depression and sedation.
interactions.diagnostics: May rarely cause false-positive tricyclic antidepressant immunoassay results.

monitoring: Degree of sedation and CNS depression
Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation)
Symptoms of serotonin syndrome when used with serotonergic agents
counsel: May cause drowsiness; do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives while taking this medicine
This is a short-term treatment (up to 2-3 weeks)
Dry mouth is common; sip water or use sugar-free gum
Tell your clinician about all other medicines, especially antidepressants and MAOIs
pk: Effect persists; dosed three times daily
Store at room temperature, protect from moisture
pearls: Structurally a tricyclic - shares anticholinergic, sedative, and cardiac cautions of TCAs
Best for short-term acute muscle spasm; no proven benefit beyond 2-3 weeks
Not effective for spasticity from cerebral or spinal cord disease or cerebral palsy
Sedation makes it useful for night-time dosing in some patients
Avoid combining with MAOIs and use caution with serotonergic drugs
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered unless it is near the next dose; then skip it. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Overdose resembles tricyclic toxicity: drowsiness, tachycardia, arrhythmias, hypotension, seizures, anticholinergic effects, and cardiac arrest. Treat with supportive care, cardiac monitoring, activated charcoal, and TCA-overdose protocols; do not give flumazenil.
